title: Entorhinal Stellate Cells
intro: Stellate cells in layer 2 of the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) are the main source of the perforant path to the dentate gyrus and CA3, and many of them are grid cells: they fire at the vertices of a triangular lattice that tiles the environment. Their membranes resonate at theta frequencies through an h-current, a property that made them the starting point for models that try to explain grid cells from single-cell dynamics, and their network is the starting point for the attractor models that won out.

items: Morphology: several primary dendrites of similar thickness radiating from the soma, without a dominant apical dendrite; spiny. Layer 2 also contains pyramidal cells, and the two differ in markers: stellate cells express reelin, the pyramidal cells calbindin, and calbindin cells cluster into 'islands' (Kitamura et al. 2014; Ray et al. 2014).

Intrinsic properties: a large, fast h-current gives a pronounced sag and rebound and a subthreshold resonance in the theta range (about 4 to 12 Hz); together with a persistent sodium current it produces subthreshold membrane potential oscillations (Alonso & Llinas 1989; Alonso & Klink 1993). The resonance frequency and h-current kinetics vary along the dorsal-ventral axis, in step with grid spacing (Giocomo et al. 2007; Garden et al. 2008).

Grid cells: Hafting et al. (2005) found MEC neurons whose firing fields form a hexagonal grid. Spacing grows from about 30 cm dorsally to several metres ventrally, in discrete modules with a ratio near 1.4 between successive modules (Stensola et al. 2012). Both stellate and pyramidal cells can be grid cells (Domnisoru, Kinkhabwala & Tank 2013; Rowland et al. 2018).

Connectivity: stellate cells hardly excite each other directly; they interact mainly through inhibitory interneurons, mostly PV cells (Couey et al. 2013; Pastoll et al. 2013). This matters for the network models below.
Outputs: the perforant path to the dentate gyrus and CA3. Layer 3 pyramidal cells project to CA1.

Single-cell conductance models: Fransen et al. (2004) and Dickson et al. (2000) built HH-type stellate models with h-current and persistent sodium that reproduce subthreshold oscillations and resonance; Alonso and Klink (1993) characterised the data they were fitted to.

Oscillatory interference models: Burgess, Barry and O'Keefe (2007) and Hasselmo, Giocomo and Zilli (2007) proposed that grid fields arise from interference between dendritic oscillators whose frequency depends on running velocity, using the intrinsic theta oscillation of stellate cells. They explain the link between resonance frequency and grid spacing, but whole-cell recordings in behaving mice (Domnisoru et al. 2013; Schmidt-Hieber & Hausser 2013) found ramp-like depolarisations in fields rather than interference patterns, and grid cells exist in bats without continuous theta (Yartsev, Witter & Ulanovsky 2011), which weighs against them.

Continuous attractor network models: Fuhs and Touretzky (2006), McNaughton et al. (2006) and Burak and Fiete (2009) showed that a sheet of neurons with centre-surround recurrent connectivity forms a stable hexagonal activity pattern, which velocity input moves to perform path integration. Pastoll et al. (2013) and Couey et al. (2013) showed that the inhibition-only connectivity of stellate cells is enough for such an attractor. Grid cell population recordings show the torus-shaped activity manifold that these models predict (Gardner et al. 2022).

Learning models: grid patterns emerge from place-like input with Hebbian learning and adaptation (Kropff & Treves 2008) and, in trained recurrent networks, from path-integration objectives (Banino et al. 2018; Sorscher et al. 2019).
Izhikevich resonator preset: a = 0.1, b = 0.26 gives subthreshold oscillations and frequency preference, a point-model stand-in for stellate resonance.

blocks.text: The resonator preset of the Izhikevich model has a fast recovery variable (a = 0.1) coupled strongly to v (b = 0.26), so its resting state is a damped oscillator rather than a simple leak, the point-neuron analogue of a stellate cell's h-current resonance. At I = 1 it already fires a steady rhythm, while the regular-spiking preset needs about four times the current before it fires at all; watch u swing up and down with v between spikes. Showing the frequency preference itself needs oscillating input at different frequencies, which this widget does not provide (the Neuronal Dynamics page, #/neuroscience/neuronal-dynamics, explains, with phase planes, why class 2 neurons near a Hopf bifurcation have subthreshold oscillations).
What this means for your SNN

items: If your column needs a location signal, the biologically grounded generator is a continuous attractor network of grid cells in several modules, driven by velocity. Grid and Displacement Cells (#/computational-cortical-columns/thousand-brains/grid-and-displacement-cells) shows how the Thousand Brains Theory reuses it.
You can build the attractor with excitatory cells connected only through inhibitory interneurons, as in the real MEC, which is easier to keep stable than direct excitatory recurrence.
Use several modules with a spacing ratio near 1.4: a combination of modules encodes position over a range much larger than any single grid's spacing.
Resonance is cheap to add (a resonator Izhikevich cell, or an h-current) if you want cells that prefer theta-rate input.
